fellowship: 1. The state or relation of being or associate. 2. Companionship of persons on equal and friendly terms; frequent and familiar intercourse. In a great town, friends are scattered, so that there is… | (Eccl.) To acknowledge as of good standing, or in communion according to standards of faith and practice; to admit to Christian fellowship.
felly: , adv. In a fell or cruel manner; fiercely; barbarously; savagely. Spenser. | The exterior wooden rim, or a segment of the rim, of a wheel, supported by the spokes. [Written also felloe.] Break all the spokes and fellies from her wheel. Shak.
fenks: The refuse whale blubber, used as a manure, and in the manufacture of Prussian blue. Ure.
febrifugal: Having the quality of mitigating or curing fever. Boyle.
felony: 1. (Feudal Law) An act on the part of the vassal which cost him his fee by forfeiture. Burrill. 2. (O.Eng.Law) An offense which occasions a total forfeiture either lands or goods, or both, at the common law, and to which capital or other punishment may be added, according to the degree of guilt. 3. A heinous crime; especially, a crime punishable by death or imprisonment.
fen: Low land overflowed, or covered wholly or partially with water, but producing sedge, coarse grasses, or other aquatic plants; boggy land; moor; marsh. 'Mid reedy fens wide spread. Wordsworth. Note: Fen is used adjectively with the sense of belonging to, or of the nature of, a fen or fens. Fen boat, a boat of light draught used in marshes.
fecundity: 1. The quality or power of producing fruit; fruitfulness; especially (Biol.), the quality in female organisms of reproducing rapidly and in great numbers. 2. The power of germinating; as in seeds. 3. The power of bringing forth in abundance; fertility; richness of invention; as, the fecundity of God's creative power. Bentley.
ferme: Rent for a farm; a farm; also, an abode; a place of residence; as, he let his land to ferm. (old) Out of her fleshy ferme fled to the place of pain. Spenser.
fenny: Pertaining to, or inhabiting, a fen; abounding in fens; swampy; boggy. "Fenny snake." Shak.
feuar: One who holds a feu. Sir W. Scott.
feebleness: The quality or condition of being feeble; debility; infirmity. That shakes for age and feebleness. Shak.
feel: 1. To perceive by the touch; to take cognizance of by means of the nerves of sensation distributed all over the body, especially by those of the skin; to have sensation excited by contact of (a… | 1. To have perception by the touch, or by contact of anything with the nerves of sensation, especially those upon the surface of the body. 2. To have the sensibilities moved or affected.
fetlock: The cushionlike projection, bearing a tuft of long hair, on the back side of the leg above the hoof of the horse and similar animals. Also, the joint of the limb at this point (between the great pastern bone and the metacarpus), or the tuft of hair. Their wounded steeds Fret fetlock deep in gore. Shak.
feuilltonist: A writer of feuilletons. F. Harrison.
ferrandine: A stuff made of silk and wool. I did buy a colored silk ferrandine. Pepys.
feldspathose: Pertaining to, or consisting of, feldspar.
fellow: 1. A companion; a comrade; an associate; a partner; a sharer. The fellows of his crime. Milton. We are fellows still, Serving alike in sorrow. Shak. That enormous engine was flanked by two fellows… | To suit with; to pair with; to match. (old) Shak.
felicity: 1. The state of being happy; blessedness; blissfulness; enjoyment of good. Our own felicity we make or find. Johnson. Finally, after this life, to attain everlasting joy and felicity. Book of Common Prayer. 2. That which promotes happiness; a successful or gratifying event; prosperity; blessing. the felicities of her wonderful reign. Atterbury. 3.
feria: A week day, esp. a day which is neither a festival nor a fast. Shipley.
ferricyanic: Pertaining to, or derived from, a ferricyanide. Ferricyanic acid (Chem.), a brown crystalline substance, H6(CN)12Fe2, obtained from potassium ferricyanide, and regarded as the type of the ferricyanides; -- called also hydro-ferricyanic acid, hydrogen ferricyanide, etc.
fernticle: A freckle on the skin, resembling the seed of fern. [Prov. Eng.]
feigning: That feigns; insincere; not genuine; false. -- Feign"ing*ly, adv.
ferula: 1. A ferule. (old) Beau. & Fl. 2. The imperial scepter in the Byzantine or Eastern Empire.
fetal: Pertaining to, or connected with, a fetus; as, fetal circulation; fetal membranes.
festivous: Pertaining to a feast; festive. Sir W. Scott.
ferric: Pertaining to, derived from, or containing iron. Specifically (Chem.), denoting those compounds in which iron has a higher valence than in the ferrous compounds; as, ferric oxide; ferric acid. Ferric acid (Chem.), an acid, H2FeO4, which is not known in the free state, but forms definite salts, analogous to the chromates and sulphates.
festucous: Formed or consisting of straw. (old) Sir T. Browne.
fertilize: 1. To make fertile or enrich; to supply with nourishment for plants; to make fruitful or productive; as, to fertilize land, soil, ground, and meadows. And fertilize the field that each pretends to gain. Byron. 2. To fecundate; as, to fertilize flower. A. R. Wallace.
fellness: The quality or state of being fell or cruel; fierce barbarity. Spenser.
femme: A woman. See Feme, n. Femme de chambre. Etym: [F.] A lady's maid; a chambermaid.
featherness: The state or condition of being feathery.
feud: 1. A combination of kindred to avenge injuries or affronts, done or offered to any of their blood, on the offender and all his race. 2. A contention or quarrel; especially, an inveterate strife… | A stipendiary estate in land, held of superior, by service; the right which a vassal or tenant had to the lands or other immovable thing of his lord, to use the same and take the profists thereof…
feminize: To make womanish or effeminate. Dr. H. More.
felonwort: The bittersweet nightshade (Solanum Dulcamara). See Bittersweet.
femininerhyme: See Female rhyme, under Female, a. Syn. -- See Female, a.
feathering: 1. (Arch.) Same as Foliation. 2. The act of turning the blade of the oar, as it rises from the water in rowing, from a vertical to a horizontal position. See To feather an oar, under Feather, v. t. 3. A covering of feathers. Feathering float (Naut.), the float or paddle of a feathering wheel.
feastful: Festive; festal; joyful; sumptuous; luxurious. "Feastful days." Milton. -- Feast"ful*ly, adv.
fettered: Seeming as if fettered, as the feet pf certain animals which bend backward, and appear unfit for walking.
festival: A time of feasting or celebration; an anniversary day of joy, civil or religious. The morning trumpets festival proclaimed. Milton. Syn. -- Feast; banquet; carousal. See Feast.
fettle: 1. To repair; to prepare; to put in order. [Prov. Eng.] Carlyle. 2. (Metal.) To cover or line with a mixture of ore, cinders, etc., as the hearth of a puddling furnace. | To make preparations; to put things in order; to do trifling business. [Prov. Eng.] Bp. Hall.
fecial: Pertaining to heralds, declarations of war, and treaties of peace; as, fecial law. Kent.
feracity: The state of being feracious or fruitful. (old) Beattie.
fetich: 1. A material object supposed among certain African tribes to represent in such a way, or to be so connected with, a supernatural being, that the possession of it gives to the possessor power to control that being. 2. Any object to which one is excessively devoted.
fetidness: The quality or state of being fetid.
fenestral: 1. (Arch.) Pertaining to a window or to windows. 2. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to a fenestra. | A casement or window sash, closed with cloth or paper instead of glass. Weale.
fermentable: Capable of fermentation; as, cider and other vegetable liquors are fermentable.
femininity: 1. The quality or nature of the female sex; womanliness. 2. The female form. (old) O serpent under femininitee. Chaucer.
fervor: 1. Heat; excessive warmth. The fevor of ensuing day. Waller. 2. Intensity of feeling or expression; glowing ardor; passion; holy zeal; earnestness. Hooker. Winged with fervor of her love. Shak. Syn. -- Fervor, Ardor. Fervor is a boiling heat, and ardor is a burning heat.
feathered: 1. Clothed, covered, or fitted with (or as with) feathers or wings; as, a feathered animal; a feathered arrow. Rise from the ground like feathered Mercury. Shak. Nonsense feathered with soft and delicate phrases and pointed with pathetic accent. Dr. J. Scott. 2. Furnished with anything featherlike; ornamented; fringed; as, land feathered with trees. 3.
fellowlike: Like a companion; companionable; on equal terms; sympathetic. (old) Udall.
felsite: A finegrained rock, flintlike in fracture, consisting essentially of orthoclase feldspar with occasional grains of quartz.
fetch: 1. To bear toward the person speaking, or the person or thing from whose point of view the action is contemplated; to go and bring; to get. Time will run back and fetch the age of gold. Milton. | To bring one's self; to make headway; to veer; as, to fetch about; to fetch to windward. Totten. To fetch away (Naut.), to break loose; to roll slide to leeward. -- To fetch and carry, to serve…
felonious: Having the quality of felony; malignant; malicious; villainous; traitorous; perfidious; in a legal sense, done with intent to commit a crime; as, felonious homicide. fertilization: 1. The act or process of rendering fertile. 2. (Biol.) The act of fecundating or impregnating animal or vegetable germs; esp., the process by which in flowers the pollen renders the ovule fertile, or an analogous process in flowerless plants; fecundation; impregnation.
feminity: Womanliness; femininity. (old) "Trained up in true feminity." Spenser.
feofor: One who enfeoffs or grants a fee.
fellowcommoner: A student at Cambridge University, England, who commons, or dines, at the Fellow's table.
felon: 1. (Law) A person who has committed a felony. 2. A person guilty or capable of heinous crime. 3. (Med.) Vain shows of love to vail his felon hate. Pope.
fergusonite: A mineral of a brownish black color, essentially a tantalo- niobate of yttrium, erbium, and cerium; -- so called after Robert Ferguson.
festlich: Festive; fond of festive occasions. (old) "A festlich man." Chaucer.
ferriswheel: An amusement device consisting of a giant power-driven steel wheel, revolvable on its stationary axle, and carrying a number of balanced passenger cars around its rim; -- so called after G. W. G. Ferris, American engineer, who erected the first of its kind for the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893.
feeling: 1. Possessing great sensibility; easily affected or moved; as, a feeling heart. 2. festoon: 1. A garland or wreath hanging in a depending curve, used in decoration for festivals, etc.; anything arranged in this way. 2. (Arch. & Sculp.) A carved ornament consisting of flowers, and leaves,… | To form in festoons, or to adorn with festoons.
fencer: One who fences; one who teaches or practices the art of fencing with sword or foil. As blunt as the fencer's foils. Shak.
feoff: , v. t. [imp. & p. p. Feoffed; p. pr. & vb. n.. Feoffing.] Etym: [OE. feffen, OF. feffer, fieffer, F. fieffer, fr. fief fief; cf. LL. feoffare, fefare. See Fief.] (Law) To invest with a fee or feud; to give or grant a corporeal hereditament to; to enfeoff.
fearsome: 1. Frightful; causing fear [Scotch] "This fearsome wind." Sir W. Scott 2 . Easily frightened; timid; timorous. "A silly fearsome thing." B. Taylor
ferment: 1. That which causes fermentation, as yeast, barm, or fermenting beer. Note: Ferments are of two kinds: (a) Formed or organized ferments. feat: 1. An act; a deed; an exploit. The warlike feats I have done. Shak. 2. A striking act of strength, skill, or cunning; a trick; as, feats of horsemanship, or of dexterity. | To form; to fashion. (old) To the more mature, A glass that feated them. Shak.
fellmonger: A dealer in fells or sheepskins, who separates the wool from the pelts.
fetter: 1. A chain or shackle for the feet; a chain by which an animal is confined by the foot, either made fast or disabled from free and rapid motion; a bond; a shackle. | 1. To put fetters upon; to shakle or confine the feet of with a chain; to bind. My heels are fettered, but my fist is free. Milton. 2. To reastrain from motion; to impose restrains on; to confine;
feather: 1. One of the peculiar dermal appendages, of several kinds, belonging to birds, as contour feathers, quills, and down. Note: An ordinary feather consists of the quill or hollow basal part of the… | 1. To furnish with a feather or feathers, as an arrow or a cap. An eagle had the ill hap to be struck with an arrow feathered from her own wing. L'Estrange. 2. To adorn, as with feathers; to fringe.
fencible: Capable of being defended, or of making or affording defense. (old) No fort so fencible, nor walls so strong. Spenser.
feneration: The act of fenerating; interest. (old) Sir T. Browne.
few: Not many; small, limited, or confined in number; -- indicating a small portion of units or individuals constituing a whole; often, by ellipsis of a noun, a few people. "Are not my days few" Job x. 20. Few know and fewer care. Proverb. Note: Few is often used partitively; as, few of them. A few, a small number. -- In few, in a few words; briefly. Shak. - No few, not few;
fertilizer: 1. One who fertilizes; the agent that carries the fertilizing principle, as a moth to an orchid. A. R. Wallace. 2. That which renders fertile; a general name for commercial manures, as guano, phosphate of lime, etc.
ferrumination: The soldering ir uniting of me Coleridge.
feticide: The act of killing the fetus in the womb; the offense of procuring an abortion.
ferule: A flat piece of wood, used for striking, children, esp. on the hand, in punishment.
featherfoil: An aquatic plant (Hottonia palustris), having finely divided leaves.
ferae: A group of mammals which formerly included the Carnivora, Insectivora, Marsupialia, and lemurs, but is now often restricted to the Carnivora.
festal: Of or pertaining to a holiday or a feast; joyous; festive. You bless with choicer wine the festal day. Francis.
fescue: 1. A straw, wire, stick, etc., used chiefly to point out letters to children when learning to read. "Pedantic fescue.' Sterne. To come under the fescue of an imprimatur. Milton. 2. | To use a fescue, or teach with a fescue. Milton.
ferding: A measure of land mentioned in Domesday Book. It is supposed to have consisted of a few acres only. (old)
featherbone: A substitute for whalebone, made from the quills of geese and turkeys.
feme: A woman. Burrill. Feme covert (Law), a married woman. See Covert, a., 3. -- Feme sole (Law), a single or unmarried woman; a woman who has never been married, or who has been divorced, or whose husband is dead. -- Feme sole trader or merchant (Eng. Law), a married woman, by the custom of London, engages in business on her own account, inpendently of her husband.
feroher: A symbol of the solar deity, found on monuments exhumed in Babylon, Nineveh, etc.
feline: 1. (Zoöl.) Catlike; of or pertaining to the genus Felis, or family Felidæ; as, the feline race; feline voracity. 2. Characteristic of cats; sly; stealthy; treacherous; as, a feline nature; feline manners.
feverish: 1. Having a fever; suffering from, or affected with, a moderate degree of fever; showing increased heat and thirst; as, the patient is feverish. 2. Indicating, or pertaining to, fever; characteristic of a fever; as, feverish symptoms. 3. Hot; sultry. "The feverish north." Dryden. 4. Disordered as by fever; excited; restless; as, the feverish condition of the commercial world.
feeder: 1. One who, or that which, gives food or supplies nourishment; steward. A couple of friends, his chaplain and feeder. Goldsmith. 2. One who furnishes incentives; an encourager. "The feeder of my riots." Shak. 3. One who eats or feeds; specifically, an animal to be fed or fattened. With eager feeding, food doth choke the feeder. Shak. 4. One who fattens cattle for slaughter. 5.
felicify: To make happy; to felicitate. (old) Quarles.
ferrocalcite: Limestone containing a large percentage of iron carbonate, and hence turning brown on exposure.
femur: (a) The thigh bone. (b) The proximal segment of the hind limb containing the thigh bone; the thigh. See Coxa.
fetishist: A believer in fetiches. He was by nature a fetichist. H. Holbeach. | See Fetich, n., Fetichism, n., Fetichistic, a.
featly: Neatly; dexterously; nimbly. (old) Foot featly here and there. Shak.
felucca: A small, swift-sailing vessel, propelled by oars and lateen sails, -- once common in the Mediterranean. Note: Sometimes it is constructed so that the helm may be used at either end.
ferrotype: A photographic picture taken on an iron plate by a collodion process; -- familiarly called tintype.
ferri: A combining form indicating ferric iron as an ingredient; as, ferricyanide.
fermentation: 1. The process of undergoing an effervescent change, as by the action of yeast; in a wider sense (Physiol. federate: United by compact, as sovereignties, states, or nations; joined in confederacy; leagued; confederate; as, federate nations.
feverous: 1. Affected with fever or ague; feverish. His heart, love's feverous citadel. Keats. 2. Pertaining to, or having the nature of, fever; as, a feverous pulse. All maladies . . . all feverous kinds. Milton. 3. Having the tendency to produce fever; as, a feverous disposition of the year. Bacon.
femalefern: a common species of fern with large decompound fronds (Asplenium Filixfæmina), growing in many countries; lady fern. Note: The names male fern and female fern were anciently given to two common ferns; but it is now understood that neither has any sexual character. Syn. -- Female, Feminine. We apply female to the sex or individual, as opposed to male;
ferruginous: 1. Partaking of iron; containing particles of iron. Boyle. 2. Resembling iron rust in appearance or color; brownish red, or yellowish red.
ferier: , compar. of Fere, fierce. (old) Rhenus ferier than the cataract. Marston.
fetichistic: Pertaining to, or involving, fetichism. A man of the fifteenth century, inheriting its strange web of belief and unbelief, of epicurean levity and fetichistic dread. G. Eliot.
federative: Uniting in a league; forming a confederacy; federal. "A federative society." Burke.
feazings: The unlaid or ragged end of a rope. Ham. Nav. Encyc.
fern: Ancient; old. (old) "Pilgrimages to . . . ferne halwes." [saints]. Chaucer. | An order of cryptogamous plants, the Filices, which have their fructification on the back of the fronds or leaves. They are usually found in humid soil, sometimes grow epiphytically on trees, and in…
featbodied: Having a feat or trim body. (old) Beau. & Fl.
fecula: Any pulverulent matter obtained from plants by simply breaking down the texture, washing with water, and subsidence. Especially: (a) The nutritious part of wheat; starch or farina; -- called also amylaceous fecula. (b) The green matter of plants; chlorophyll.
feigned: Not real or genuine; pretended; counterfeit; insincere; false. "A feigned friend." Shak. Give ear unto my prayer, that goeth not out of feigned lips. federary: A partner; a confederate; an accomplice. (old) hak.
ferreous: Partaking of, made of, or pertaining to, iron; like iron. (old) Sir T. Browne.
federalize: To unite in compact, as different States; to confederate for political purposes; to unite by or under the Federal Constitution. Barlow.
febrifacient: Febrific. Dunglison. -- n. That which causes fever. Beddoes.
felis: A genus of carnivorous mammals, including the domestic cat, the lion, tiger, panther, and similar animals.
feodary: 1. An accomplice. Art thou a feodary for this act Shak. 2. (Eng. Law) An ancient officer of the court of wards. Burrill.
ferro: A prefix, or combining form, indicating ferrous iron as an ingredient; as, ferrocyanide.
felicitation: The act of felicitating; a wishing of joy or happiness; congratulation.
feldspar: A name given to a group of minerals, closely related in crystalline form, and all silicates of alumina with either potash, soda, lime, or, in one case, baryta. They occur in crystals and crystalline masses, vitreous in luster, and breaking rather easily in two directions at right angles to each other, or nearly so.
feed: 1. To give food to; to supply with nourishment; to satisfy the physical huger of. If thine enemy hunger, feed him. Rom. xii. 20. Unreasonable reatures feed their young. Shak. 2. To satisfy; | 1. To take food; to eat. Her kid . . . which I afterwards killed because it would not feed. De Foe. 2. To subject by eating; to satisfy the appetite; to feed one's self (upon something); to prey;
fetishistic: Pertaining to, or involving, fetichism. A man of the fifteenth century, inheriting its strange web of belief and unbelief, of epicurean levity and fetichistic dread. G. Eliot. | See Fetich, n., Fetichism, n., Fetichistic, a.
fetid: Having an offensive smell; stinking. Most putrefactions . . . smell either fetid or moldy. Bacon.
fewness: 1. The state of being few; smallness of number; paucity. Shak. 2. Brevity; conciseness. (old) Shak.
fester: 1. To generate pus; to become imflamed and suppurate; as, a sore or a wound festers. Wounds immedicable Rankle, and fester, and gangrene. Milton. Unkindness may give a wound that shall bleed and… | To cause to fester or rankle. For which I burnt in inward, swelt'ring hate, And fstered ranking malice in my breast. Marston.
ferulic: Pertaining to, or derived from, asafetida (Ferula asafoetida); as, ferulic acid. [Written also ferulaic.]
ferocity: Savage wildness or fierceness; fury; cruelty; as, ferocity of countenance. The pride and ferocity of a Highland chief. Macaulay.
fender: One who or that which defends or protects by warding off harm; as: (a) A screen to prevent coals or sparks of an open fire from escaping to the floor. (c) A screen to protect a carriage from mud thrown off the wheels: also, a splashboard.
fenugreek: A plant (trigonella Foenum Græcum) cultivated for its strong- smelling seeds, which are "now only used for giving false importance to horse medicine and damaged hay." J. Smith (Pop. Names of Plants, 1881).
feuilleton: A part of a French newspaper (usually the bottom of the page), devoted to light literature, criticism, etc.; also, the article or tale itself, thus printed.
fellowfeeling: 1. Sympathy; a like feeling. 2. Joint interest. (old) Arbuthnot.
feudist: A writer on feuds; a person versed in feudal law. Spelman.
ferocious: Fierce; savage; wild; indicating cruelty; ravenous; rapacious; as, ferocious look or features; a ferocious lion. The humbled power of a ferocious enemy. Lowth. fenceless: Without a fence; uninclosed; open; unguarded; defenseless. Milton.
ferial: 1. Of or pertaining to holidays. (old) J. Gregory. 2. Belonging to any week day, esp. to a day that is neither a festival nor a fast.
fear: A variant of Fere, a mate, a companion. (old) Spenser. | 1. A painful emotion or passion excited by the expectation of evil, or the apprehension of impending danger; apprehension; anxiety; solicitude; alarm; dread. Note: The degrees of this passion,…
february: The second month in the year, said to have been introduced into the Roman calendar by Numa. In common years this month contains twenty-eight days; in the bissextile, or leap year, it has twenty- nine days.
fez: A felt or cloth cap, usually red and having a tassel, -- a variety of the tarboosh. See Tarboosh. B. Taylor.

fetichist: A believer in fetiches. He was by nature a fetichist. H. Holbeach.
fenestrate: 1. Having numerous openings; irregularly reticulated; as, fenestrate membranes; fenestrate fronds. 2. (Zoöl.) Having transparent spots, as the wings of certain butterflies.

fecundify: To make fruitful; to fecundate. Johnson.
fellah: A peasant or cultivator of the soil among the Egyptians, Syrians, etc. W. M. Thomson.

ferly: Singular; wonderful; extraordinary. (old) -- n. A wonder; a marvel. (old) Who hearkened ever such a ferly thing. Chaucer.

feuillants: A reformed branch of the Bernardines, founded in 1577 at Feuillans, near Toulouse, in France.
ferrary: The art of working in iron. (old) Chapman.
feasible: 1. Capable of being done, executed, or effected; practicable. Always existing before their eyes as a thing feasible in practice. Burke. It was not feasible to gratify so many ambitions. Beaconsfield. 2. Fit to be used or tailed, as land. R. Trumbull. Fea"si*ble*ness, n. --Fea"si*bly, adv.

feculent: Foul with extraneous or impure substances; abounding with sediment or excrementitious matter; muddy; thick; turbid. Both his hands most filthy feculent. Spenser.
fervid: 1. Very hot; burning; boiling. The mounted sun Shot down direct his fervid rays. Milton. 2. Ardent; vehement; zealous. The fervid wishes, holy fires. Parnell. -- Fer"vid*ly, adv. -- Fer"vid*ness, n.
feudal: 1. Of or pertaining to feuds, fiefs, or feels; as, feudal rights or services; feudal tenures. 2. Consisting of, or founded upon, feuds or fiefs; embracing tenures by military services; as, the feudal system.
ferriage: The price or fare to be paid for passage at a ferry.
ferret: An animal of the Weasel family (Mustela or Putorius furo), about fourteen inches in length, of a pale yellow or white color, with red eyes. It is a native of Africa, but has been domesticated in… | To drive or hunt out of a lurking place, as a ferret does the cony; to search out by patient and sagacious efforts; -- often used with out; as, to ferret out a secret.
feodality: Feudal tenure; the feudal system. See Feudality. Burke.
fettling: 1. (Metal.) A mixture of ore, cinders, etc., used to line the hearth of a puddling furnace. [Eng.] [It is commonly called fix in the United States.] 2. (Pottery) The operation of shaving or smoothing the surface of undried clay ware.
fengite: A kind of marble or alabaster, sometimes used for windows on account of its transparency.
feoffer: One who enfeoffs or grants a fee.
fecundate: 1. To make fruitful or prolific. W. Montagu. 2. (Biol.) To render fruitful or prolific; to impregnate; as, in flowers the pollen fecundates the ovum through the stigma.
febriferous: Causing fever; as, a febriferous locality.
fervent: 1. Hot; glowing; boiling; burning; as, a fervent summer. The elements shall melt with fervent heat. 2 Pet. iii. 10. 2. Warm in feeling; ardent in temperament; earnest; full of fervor; zealous; glowing. Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit. Rom. iii. 11. So spake the fervent angel. Milton. A fervent desire to promote the happiness of mankind. Macaulay.
feraenaturae: Of a wild nature; -- applied to animals, as foxes, wild ducks, etc., in which no one can claim property.
feeze: 1. To turn, as a screw. [Scot] Jamieson. 2. To beat; to chastise; to humble; to worry. (old) [Written also feaze, feize, pheese.] Beau. & Fl. To feeze up, to work into a passion. (old) | Fretful excitement. (old) See Feaze.
feudalization: The act of reducing to feudal tenure.
ferruginated: Having the color or properties of the rust of iron.
fencing: 1. The art or practice of attack and defense with the sword, esp. with the s,allword. See Fence, v. i., 2. 2. Disputing or debating in a manner resembling the art of fencers. Shak. 3. The materials used for building fences. [U.S.] 4. The act of building a fence. 5. To aggregate of the fences put up for inclosure or protection; as, the fencing of a farm.
fertilitate: To fertilize; to fecundate. Sir T. Browne.
feudejoie: A fire kindled in a public place in token of joy; a bonfire; a firing of guns in token of joy.
fenestrule: One of the openings in a fenestrated structure.
feetless: Destitute of feet; as, feetless birds.
fenestella: Any small windowlike opening or recess, esp. one to show the relics within an altar, or the like.
ferryman: One who maintains or attends a ferry.
feoffment: (a) The grant of a feud or fee. (b) (Eng. Law) A gift or conveyance in fee of land or other corporeal hereditaments, accompanied by actual delivery of possession. Burrill. (c) The instrument or deed by which corporeal hereditaments are conveyed. [Obs. in the U.S., Rare in Eng.]
fenestrated: 1. (Arch.) Having windows; characterized by windows. 2. Same as Fenestrate.
feathery: Pertaining to, or resembling, feathers; covered with, or as with, feathers; as, feathery spray or snow. Milton. Ye feathery people of mid air. Barry Cornwall.
featheredged: Having a feather-edge; also, having one edge thinner than the other, as a board; -- in the United States, said only of stuff one edge of which is made as thin as practicable.
feere: A consort, husband or wife; a companion; a fere. (old)
ferrara: A sword bearing the mark of one of the Ferrara family of Italy. These swords were highly esteemed in England and Scotland in the 16th and 17th centuries.
federalism: the principles of Federalists or of federal union.
felodese: One who deliberately puts an end to his own existence, or loses his life while engaged in the commission of an unlawful or malicious act; a suicide. Burrill.
feu: A free and gratuitous right to lands made to one for service to be performed by him; a tenure where the vassal, in place of military services, makes a return in grain or in money. Burrill.
ferulaceous: Pertaining to reeds and canes; having a stalk like a reed; as, ferulaceous plants.
fealty: 1. Fidelity to one's lord; the feudal obligation by which the tenant or vassal was bound to be faithful to his lord; the special oath by which this obligation was assumed; fidelity to a superior power, or to a government; loyality. It is no longer the practice to exact the performance of fealty, as a feudal obligation. Wharton (Law Dict. ). Tomlins. 2. Fidelity; constancy;
ferforth: Far forth. (old) As ferforth as, as far as. -- So ferforth, to such a degree.
feign: 1. To give a mental existence to, as to something not real or actual; to imagine; to invent; hence, to pretend; to form and relate as if true. There are no such things done as thou sayest, but thou feignest them out of thine own heart. Neh. vi. 8. The poet Did feign that Orpheus drew trees, stones, and floods. Shak. 2. To represent by a false appearance of; to pretend;
feldspathic: Pertaining to, or consisting of, feldspar.
felting: 1. The material of which felt is made; also, felted cloth; also, the process by which it is made. 2. The act of splitting timber by the felt grain.
feaster: 1. One who fares deliciously. 2. One who entertains magnificently. Johnson.
felsitic: relating to, composed of, or containing, felsite.
feese: the short run before a leap. (old) Nares.
feudalize: To reduce toa feudal tenure; to conform to feudalism.
felicitate: Made very happy. (old) I am alone felicitate In your dear highness' love. Shak. | 1. To make very happy; to delight. What a glorius entertainment and pleasure would fill and felicitate his spirit. I. Watts. 2. To express joy or pleasure to; to wish felicity to;
feudary: Held by, or pertaining to, feudal tenure. | 1. A tenant who holds his lands by feudal service; a feudatory. Foxe. 2. A feodary. See Feodary.
femalize: To make, or to describe as, female or feminine. Shaftesbury.
featherhead: A frivolous or featherbrained person. [Colloq.] H. James.
fecal: relating to, or containing, dregs, feces, or ordeure; fæcal.
festucine: Of a straw color; greenish yellow. (old) A little insect of a festucine or pale green. Sir T. Browne.
feriation: The act of keeping holiday; cessation from work. (old) Sir T. Browne.
fetis: Neat; pretty; well made; graceful. (old) Full fetis was her cloak, as I was ware. Chaucer.
fenestration: 1. (Arch.) The arrangement and proportioning of windows; -- used by modern writers for the decorating of an architectural composition by means of the window (and door) openings, their ornaments, and proportions. 2. (Anat.) The state or condition of being fenestrated.
fellowless: Without fellow or equal; peerless. Whose well-built walls are rare and fellowless. Chapman.
feltgrain: , the grain of timber which is transverse to the annular rings or plates; the direction of the medullary rays in oak and some other timber. Knight.
ferm: Rent for a farm; a farm; also, an abode; a place of residence; as, he let his land to ferm. (old) Out of her fleshy ferme fled to the place of pain. Spenser.
ferry: To carry or transport over a river, strait, or other narrow water, in a boat. | To pass over water in a boat or by a ferry. They ferry over this Lethean sound Both to and fro. Milton.
fertility: The state or quality of being fertile or fruitful; fruitfulness; productiveness; fecundity; richness; abundance of resources; fertile invention; quickness; readiness; as, the fertility of soil, or of imagination. "fertility of resource." E. Everett. And all her husbandry doth lie on heaps Corrupting in its own fertility. Shak. Thy very weeds are beautiful;
ferreteye: The spur-winged goose; -- so called from the red circle around the eyes.
ferous: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.
feefawfum: A nonsensical exclamation attributed to giants and ogres; hence, any expression calculated to impose upon the timid and ignorant. "Impudent fee-faw-fums." J. H. Newman.
fenowed: Corrupted; decayed; moldy. See Vinnewed. (old) Dr. Favour.
feudality: The state or quality of being feudal; feudal form or constitution. Burke.
feuillemort: Having the color of a faded leaf. Locke.
fennec: A small, African, foxlike animal (Vulpes zerda) of a pale fawn color, remarkable for the large size of its ears.
feeding: 1. the act of eating, or of supplying with food; the process of fattening. 2. That which is eaten; food. 3. That which furnishes or affords food, especially for animals; pasture land. Feeding bottle. See under Bottle.
ferrocyanide: One of a series of complex double cyanides of ferrous iron and some other base. Potassium ferrocyanide (Chem.), yellow prussiate of potash; a tough, yellow, crystalline salt, K4(CN)6Fe, the starting point in the manufacture of almost all cyanogen compounds, and the basis of the ferric ferrocyanate, prussian blue.
feast: 1. A festival; a holiday; a solemn, or more commonly, a joyous, anniversary. The seventh day shall be a feast to the Lord. Ex. xiii. 6. Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of… | 1. To eat sumptuously; to dine or sup on rich provisions, particularly in large companies, and on public festivals. And his sons went and feasted in their houses. Job. i. 4. 2.
feminine: 1. Of or pertaining to a woman, or to women; characteristic of a woman; womanish; womanly. Her letters are remarkably deficient in feminine ease and grace. Macaulay. 2. | 1. A woman. [Obs. or Colloq.] They guide the feminines toward the palace. Hakluyt. 2. (Gram.) Any one of those words which are the appellations of females, or which have the terminations usually…
ferricyanate: A salt of ferricyanic acid; a ferricyanide.
fearless: Free from fear. Syn. -- Bold; courageous; interpid; valor -- Fear"less*ly, adv. -- Fera"less*ness, n.
fecundation: The act by which, either in animals or plants, material prepared by the generative organs the female organism is brought in contact with matter from the organs of the male, so that a new organism results; impregnation; fertilization.
fenestra: A small opening; esp., one of the apertures, closed by membranes, between the tympanum and internal ear.
fenianism: The principles, purposes, and methods of the Fenians.
fellowfeel: To share through sympathy; to participate in. D. Rodgers.
festoony: Pertaining to, consisting of, or resembling, festoons. Sir J. Herschel.
femalist: A gallant. (old) Courting her smoothly like a femalist. Marston.
federal: 1. Pertaining to a league or treaty; derived from an agreement or covenant between parties, especially between nations; constituted by a compact between parties, usually governments or their representatives. The Romans compelled them, contrary to all federal right, . . . to part with Sardinia. Grew. 2.
feral: Wild; untamed; ferine; not domesticated; -- said of beasts, birds, and plants. feral child, not raised by humans | Funereal; deadly; fatal; dangerous. "Feral accidents." Burton.
festive: Pertaining to, or becoming, a feast; festal; joyous; gay; mirthful; sportive. -- Fes"tive*ly, adv. The glad circle round them yield their souls To festive mirth and wit that knows no gall. Thomson.
fess: A band drawn horizontally across the center of an escutcheon, and containing in breadth the third part of it; one of the nine honorable ordinaries. Fess point (Her.), the exact center of the escutcheon. See Escutcheon.
fee: 1. property; possession; tenure. "Laden with rich fee." Spenser. Once did she hold the gorgeous East in fee. Wordsworth. 2. Reward or compensation for services rendered or to be rendered; | To reward for services performed, or to be performed; to recompense; to hire or keep in hire; hence, to bribe. The patient . . . fees the doctor. Dryden. There's not a one of them but in his house I…
febrifuge: A medicine serving to mitigate or remove fever. -- a. Antifebrile.
ferrantiphenomenon: An increase in the ratio of transformation of an alternating current converter, accompanied by other changes in electrical conditions, occurring when the secondary of the converter is connected with a condenser of moderate capacity; -- so called because first observed in connection with the Ferranti cables in London.
feoffee: The person to whom a feoffment is made; the person enfeoffed.
fecifork: The anal fork on which the larvæ of certain insects carry their fæces.
fete: A festival. Fête champêtre ( Etym: [F.], a festival or entertainment in the open air; a rural festival. | To feast; to honor with a festival.
ferrocyanate: A salt of ferrocyanic acid; a ferrocyanide.
federation: 1. The act of uniting in a league; confederation. 2. A league; a confederacy; a federal or confederated government. Burke.
feculence: 1. The state or quality of being feculent; muddiness; foulness. 2. That which is feculent; sediment; lees; dregs.
feeler: 1. One who, or that which, feels. 2. (Zoöl.) One of the sense organs or certain animals (as insects), which are used in testing objects by touch and in searching for food; an antenna; a palp. Insects . . . perpetually feeling and searching before them with their feelers or antennæ. Derham. 3.
ferranticables: A form of conductor, designed by Ferranti, for currents of high potential, and consisting of concentric tubes of copper separated by an insulating material composed of paper saturated with black mineral wax.
fengshui: A system of spirit influences for good and evil believed by the Chinese to attend the natural features of landscape; also, a kind of geomancy dealing with these influences, used in determining sites for graves, houses, etc.
feeble: 1. Deficient in physical strenght; weak; infirm; debilitated. Carried all the feeble of them upon asses. 2 Chron. xxviii. 15. 2. Wanting force, vigor, or efficiency in action or expression; | To make feble; to enfeeble. (old) Shall that victorious hand be feebled here Shak.
fellon: Variant of Felon. (old) Those two were foes the fellonest on ground. Spenser.
feelingly: In a feeling manner; pathetically; sympathetically.
fearnaught: 1. A fearless person. 2. A stout woolen cloth of great thickness; dreadnaught; also, a warm garment.
featured: 1. Shaped; fashioned. How noble, young, how rarely featured! Shak. 2. Having features; formed into features. The well-stained canvas or the featured stone. Young.
fetichism: 1. The doctrine or practice of belief in fetiches. 2. Excessive devotion to one object or one idea; abject superstition; blind adoration. The real and absolute worship of fire falls into two great divisions, the first belonging rather to fetichism, the second to polytheism proper. Tylor.
femerell: A lantern, or louver covering, placed on a roof, for ventilation or escape of smoke.
fell: 1. Cruel; barbarous; inhuman; fierce; savage; ravenous. While we devise fell tortures for thy faults. Shak. 2. Eager; earnest; intent. (old) I am so fell to my business. Pepys. | Gall; anger; melancholy. (old) Untroubled of vile fear or bitter fell. Spenser.
fest: The fist. (old) Chaucer. | A feast. (old) Chaucer.
fetation: The formation of a fetus in the womb; pregnancy.
fescennine: Pertaining to, or resembling, the Fescennines. -- n. A style of low, scurrilous, obscene poetry originating in fescennia.
fever: 1. (Med.) A diseased state of the system, marked by increased heat, acceleration of the pulse, and a general derangement of the functions, including usually, thirst and loss of appetite. | To put into a fever; to affect with fever; as, a fevered lip. The white hand of a lady fever thee. Shak.
ferrous: Pertaining to, or derived from, iron; -- especially used of compounds of iron in which the iron has its lower valence; as, ferrous sulphate.
ferroconcrete: Concrete strengthened by a core or foundation skeleton of iron or steel bars, strips, etc. Floors, columns, piles, water pipes, etc., have been successfully made of it. Called also armored concrete steel, and reënforced concrete.
fetor: A strong, offensive smell; stench; fetidness. Arbuthnot.
feaze: To untwist; to unravel, as the end of a rope. Johnson. | To beat; to chastise; also, to humble; to harass; to worry. (old) insworth.
fencemonth: the month in which female deer are fawning, when hunting is prohibited. Bullokar. -- Fence roof, a covering for defense. "They fitted their shields close to one another in manner of a fence roof." Holland. Fence time, the breeding time of fish or game, when they should not be killed. -- Rail fence, a fence made of rails, sometimes supported by posts.
fence: 1. That which fends off attack or danger; a defense; a protection; a cover; security; shield. Let us be backed with God and with the seas, Which he hath given for fence impregnable. Shak. | 1. To fend off danger from; to give security to; to protect; to guard. To fence my ear against thy sorceries. Milton. 2. To inclose with a fence or other protection; to secure by an inclosure.
febrile: Pertaining to fever; indicating fever, or derived from it; as, febrile symptoms; febrile action. Dunglison.
fetish: 1. A material object supposed among certain African tribes to represent in such a way, or to be so connected with, a supernatural being, that the possession of it gives to the possessor power to… | See Fetich, n., Fetichism, n., Fetichistic, a.
featheriness: The state or condition of being feathery.
ferricyanide: One of a complex series of double cyanides of ferric iron and some other base. Potassium ferricyanide (Chem.), red prussiate of potash; a dark, red, crystalline salt, K6(CN)12Fe2, consisting of the double cyanide of potassium and ferric iron. From it is derived the ferrous ferricyanate, Turnbull's blue.
ferdelance: A large, venomous serpent (Trigonocephalus lanceolatus) of Brazil and the West Indies. It is allied to the rattlesnake, but has no rattle.
featurely: Having features; showing marked peculiarities; handsome. Featurely warriors of Christian chivalry. Coleridge.
feminye: The people called Amazons. (old) "[The reign of] feminye." Chaucer.
fenghwang: A pheasantlike bird of rich plumage and graceful form and movement, fabled to appear in the land on the accession of a sage to the throne, or when right principles are about to prevail. It is often represented on porcelains and other works of art.
feck: 1. Effect. (old) 2. Efficacy; force; value. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.] 3. Amount; quantity. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.] He had a feck o' books wi' him. R. L. Stevenson. The most feck, or The feck, the greater or larger part. "The feck o' my life." Burns.
feminization: The act of feminizing, or the state of being feminized.
fetus: The young or embryo of an animal in the womb, or in the egg; often restricted to the later stages in the development of viviparous and oviparous animals, embryo being applied to the earlier stages. [Written also foetus.]
fearful: 1. Full of fera, apprehension, or alarm; afraid; frightened. Anxious amidst all their success, and fearful amidat all their power. Bp. Warburton. 2. inclined to fear; easily frightened; without courage; timid. What man is there that is fearful and fain-hearted Deut. xx. 8. 3. Indicating, or caused by, fear. Cold fearful drops stand on my trembling flesh. Shak. 4.
federalist: An advocate of confederation; specifically (Amer. Hist.), a friend of the Constitution of the United States at its formation and adoption; a member of the political party which favored the administration of president Washington.
fermerere: The officer in a religious house who had the care of the infirmary. (old)
fetwah: A written decision of a Turkish mufti on some point of law. Whitworth.
feague: To beat or whip; to drive. (old) Otway.
feebly: In a feeble manner. The restored church . . . contended feebly, and with half a heart. Macaulay.
femoral: Pertaining to the femur or thigh; as, the femoral artery. "Femoral habiliments." Sir W. Scott.
fetishism: 1. The doctrine or practice of belief in fetiches. 2. Excessive devotion to one object or one idea; abject superstition; blind adoration. The real and absolute worship of fire falls into two great… | See Fetich, n., Fetichism, n., Fetichistic, a.
feminineness: The quality of being feminine; womanliness; womanishness.
femalerhymes: double rhymes, or rhymes (called in French feminine rhymes because they end in e weak, or feminine) in which two syllables, an accented and an unaccented one, correspond at the end of each line. Note: A rhyme, in which the final syllables only agree (strain, complain) is called a male rhyme;
ferryboat: A vessel for conveying passengers, merchandise, etc., across streams and other narrow waters.
fertile: 1. Producing fruit or vegetation in abundance; fruitful; able to produce abundantly; prolific; fecund; productive; rich; inventive; as, fertile land or fields; a fertile mind or imagination. Though he in a fertile climate dwell. Shak. 2. (Bot.) (a) Capable of producing fruit; fruit-bearing; as, fertile flowers. (b) Containing pollen; -- said of anthers. 3.
feitsui: The Chinese name for a highly prized variety of pale green jade. See Jade.
featherveined: Having the veins (of a leaf) diverging from the two sides of a midrib.
fertilely: In a fertile or fruitful manner.
fermentationtheory: The theory which likens the course of certain diseases (esp. infectious diseases) to the process of fermentation, and attributes them to the organized ferments in the body. It does not differ materially from the accepted germ theory (which see).
fesse: A band drawn horizontally across the center of an escutcheon, and containing in breadth the third part of it; one of the nine honorable ordinaries. Fess point (Her.), the exact center of the escutcheon. See Escutcheon.
fervency: The state of being fervent or warm; ardor; warmth of feeling or devotion; eagerness. When you pray, let it be with attention, with fervency, and with perseverance. Wake.
fellinic: Of, relating to, or derived from, bile or gall; as, fellinic acid.
feuter: To set close; to fix in rest, as a spear. Spenser.
fensucked: Sucked out of marches. "Fen-sucked fogs." Shak.
feller: One who, or that which, fells, knocks or cuts down; a machine for felling trees. | An appliance to a sewing machine for felling a seam.
ferrantimains: A form of conductor, designed by Ferranti, for currents of high potential, and consisting of concentric tubes of copper separated by an insulating material composed of paper saturated with black mineral wax.
ferruminate: To solder or unite, as metals. Coleridge.
fere: A mate or companion; -- often used of a wife. (old) [Written also fear and feere.] Chaucer. And Cambel took Cambrina to his fere. Spenser. In fere, together; in company. (old) Chaucer.
feudatory: A tenant or vassal who held his lands of a superior on condition of feudal service; the tenant of a feud or fief. The grantee . . . was styled the feudatory or vassal. Blackstone. | Held from another on some conditional tenure; as, a feudatory title. Bacon.
felonry: A body of felons; specifically, the convict population of a penal colony. Howitt.
festivity: 1. The condition of being festive; social joy or exhilaration of spirits at an entertaintment; joyfulness; gayety. The unrestrained festivity of the rustic youth. Bp. Hurd. 2. A festival; a festive celebration. Sir T. Browne.
feringee: The name given to Europeans by the Hindos. [Written also Feringhee.]
ferrocyanic: Pertaining to, derived from, or designating, a ferrocyanide. ferrocyanic acid (Chem.), a white crystalline substance, H4(CN)6Fe, of strong acid properties, obtained from potassium ferrocyanide, and regarded as the type of the ferrocyanides; -- called also hydro- ferrocyanic acid, hydrogen ferrocyanide. etc.
felter: To clot or mat together like felt. His feltered locks that on his bosom fell. Fairfax.
fet: To fetch. (old) And from the other fifty soon the prisoner fet. Spenser.
feint: Feigned; counterfeit. (old) Dressed up into any feint appearance of it. Locke. | 1. That which is feigned; an assumed or false appearance; a pretense; a stratagem; a fetch. Courtley's letter is but a feint to get off. Spectator. 2. A mock blow or attack on one part when another…
featheredge: 1. (Zoöl.) The thin, new growth around the edge of a shell, of an oyster. 2. Any thin, as on a board or a razor.
feature: 1. The make, form, or outward appearance of a person; the whole turn or style of the body; esp., good appearance. What needeth it his feature to descrive Chaucer. Cheated of feature by dissembling nature. Shak. 2. The make, cast, or appearance of the human face, and especially of any single part of the face; a lineament. (pl.) The face, the countenance.
ferrarese: Pertaining to Ferrara, in Italy. -- n., sing. & pl. A citizen of Ferrara; collectively, the inhabitants of Ferrara.
fenerate: To put money to usury; to lend on interest. (old) Cockeram.
felwort: A European herb (Swertia perennis) of the Gentian family.
fellowcreature: One of the same race or kind; one made by the same Creator. Reason, by which we are raised above our fellow-creatures, the brutes. I. Watts.
feldspath: A name given to a group of minerals, closely related in crystalline form, and all silicates of alumina with either potash, soda, lime, or, in one case, baryta. They occur in crystals and crystalline masses, vitreous in luster, and breaking rather easily in two directions at right angles to each other, or nearly so.
fermeture: The mechanism for closing the breech of a breech-loading firearm, in artillery consisting principally of the breechblock, obturator, and carrier ring.
female: 1. An individual of the sex which conceives and brings forth young, or (in a wider sense) which has an ovary and produces ova. The male and female of each living thing. Drayton. 2. | 1. Belonging to the sex which conceives and gives birth to young, or (in a wider sense) which produces ova; not male. As patient as the female dove When that her golden couplets are disclosed. Shak.
fey: Fated; doomed. [Old Eng. & Scot.] | To cleanse; to clean out. (old) Tusser.
feasibility: The quality of being feasible; practicability; also, that which is feasible; as, before we adopt a plan, let us consider its feasibility. Men often swallow falsities for truths, dubiosities for certainties, possibilities for feasibilities. Sir T. Browne.
feverfew: A perennial plant (Pyrethrum, or Chrysanthemum, Parthenium) allied to camomile, having finely divided leaves and white blossoms; -- so named from its supposed febrifugal qualities.
fermentative: Causing, or having power to cause, fermentation; produced by fermentation; fermenting; as, a fermentative process. -- Fer*ment"a*tive*ly, adv. -- Fer*ment"a*tive*ness, n.
ferrule: 1. A ring or cap of metal put round a cane, tool, handle, or other similar object, to strengthen it, or prevent splitting and wearing. 2. (Steam Boilers) A bushing for expanding the end of a flue to fasten it tightly in the tube plate, or for partly filling up its mouth.
feretory: A portable bier or shrine, variously adorned, used for containing relics of saints. Mollett.
fennel: A perennial plant of the genus Fæniculum (F.vulgare), having very finely divided leaves. It is cultivated in gardens for the agreeable aromatic flavor of its seeds. Smell of sweetest fennel. Milton. A sprig of fennel was in fact the theological smelling bottle of the tender sex. S. G. Goodrich. Azorean, or Sweet, fennel, (Fæniculum dulce).
feebleminded: Weak in intellectual power; wanting firmness or constancy; irresolute; vacilating; imbecile. "comfort the feeble-minded." 1 Thess. v. 14. -- Fee"ble-mind"ed*ness, n.
fearer: One who fars. Sir P. Sidney.
ferretto: Copper sulphide, used to color glass. Hebert.
featherstitch: A kind of embroidery stitch producing a branching zigzag line.
fecks: A corruption of the word faith. Shak.
feudalism: The feudal system; a system by which the holding of estates in land is made dependent upon an obligation to render military service to the kind or feudal superior; feudal principles and usages.
ferrugo: A disease of plants caused by fungi, commonly called the rust, from its resemblance to iron rust in color.
featureless: Having no distinct or distinctive features.
